final_proof:
Let $\Sigma$ be a $\sigma$-algebra on a set $X$.
By definition of a $\sigma$-algebra, $\Sigma$ is a collection of subsets of $X$ (so $\Sigma \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$) that is closed under countable unions.
Since it is closed under countable unions, it is in particular closed under finite unions.
That is, for any $A, B \in \Sigma$, their set union $A \cup B$ is also in $\Sigma$.
This implies that the binary operation of set union $\cup$ is a closed operation on $\Sigma$.
By the definition of a magma, any set equipped with a closed binary operation forms a magma. Thus, $(\Sigma, \cup)$ is a magma.
Because $\Sigma$ is a set of sets and the operation $\cup$ is a set operation, $(\Sigma, \cup)$ is a magma of sets.
Therefore, the concept of a $\sigma$-algebra is an instance of a magma of sets.
